deep.reconstruction:
Setting and purpose. Euler is computing how fast water leaves a vessel that drains through a vertical pipe when there is friction at the pipe walls. The apparatus is:
- an upper vessel of height a and cross-section ff;
- a vertical tube BC of length b and cross-section gg;
- a bottom orifice CC of area kk.
The outflow velocity is expressed as the head v (the height whose free-fall speed equals the outflow speed). l is the atmospheric pressure head, which Euler takes as 30 ft of water. α is a wall-friction coefficient.

In the friction law developed on the preceding pages, the friction per unit length is proportional to α/g times the local 'status compressionis' (the pressure head). That is why l enters the result.

The previous page gave a power series in αb/g. On this page (§48) Euler inserts his empirical estimate α ≈ 1/4000, from 'crude experiments'. He concludes that when b/g is well below 4000, first-order terms suffice:
 v(1 − (αb/g)(k⁴/g⁴)) = a + b − (αb/g)(a + b/2 + l).
To first order this gives
 v = a + b − (αb/g)[a + b/2 + l − (k⁴/g⁴)(a + b)].

§49 considers two limiting cases.
- Tiny orifice (k⁴/g⁴ ≈ 0): v = a + b − (αb/g)(a + b/2 + l). Here friction retards the flow most.
- Fully open tube (kk = gg): v = a + b − (αb/g)(l − b/2). The correction would vanish at b = 2l and would change sign beyond it.

§50 draws the consequence. With l = 30 ft, a tube longer than 60 ft would give v > a + b, i.e. friction would make the water flow faster than without friction. Euler calls this certainly impossible. He resolves it physically: the water does not stay attached to the tube wall but leaves a vacuum, so the calculation no longer applies.

The next page (§§51–53) makes this precise. The pressure at the top of the tube is, at zeroth order, R = l + a − (k⁴/g⁴)(a + b). For the open tube this requires b < l. So the paradoxical regime b ≥ 2l lies outside the domain of validity of the model.
errors: No algebraic errors. The first-order truncation of the previous page's series and the inversion of (1 − ε) are correct to O(α). The specialisations k→0 and k=g are correct.

Conceptual weakness: the apparent paradox comes from Euler's pressure-proportional (Coulomb/Amontons-type) friction law. Under that law the head loss depends on the ambient pressure l, which is unphysical for real liquid pipe flow. Euler instead defends the model by invoking separation/cavitation. That defence is consistent here (the paradox needs b = 2l, but validity already needs b < l), but it hides the defect of the friction law itself.
The value α ≈ 1/4000 is admittedly from crude, passing experiments; no data are given.

ideas.what: First-order friction correction to Torricelli outflow through a long vertical pipe. The loss is proportional to (αb/g) times a pressure-dependent factor; b/g plays the role of a length/diameter ratio.
ideas.modern_name: pipe head loss (precursor of Darcy–Weisbach L/D dependence)
ideas.where_published: E260 itself (Novi Comm. Petrop. 6, 1756/57, publ. 1761); discussed in Truesdell's introduction to Opera omnia II.12/13 (unsure of exact details)

ideas.what: Empirical estimate of the fluid wall-friction coefficient α ≈ 1/4000 from crude experiments.

The model's prediction v > a+b (friction speeding up the flow) is rejected; the domain of validity is limited by the requirement of positive pressure everywhere, otherwise the water leaves the wall and a vacuum forms.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (turbine/hydraulic machine papers of the 1750s, e.g. on Segner's wheel); later Reynolds, Parsons

missed.claim: Euler's own computation exposes an internal tension in his pressure-proportional friction law: the loss depends on atmospheric pressure l and can change sign. He diagnoses this as cavitation rather than as a flaw in the constitutive law. This is likely already noted in the literature (Truesdell), so it is probably not new.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historiographically, it shows how Euler used a physical admissibility condition (positive pressure) to delimit a model's validity. That is an early instance of checking a model's consistency against its own assumptions.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine specialisation of the series from the previous page. The cavitation/positive-pressure argument is known from Euler's hydraulic work, and E260 is covered in Truesdell's histories. The empirical α ≈ 1/4000 and the L/D-type dependence are mildly interesting but documented in the paper itself.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image well; no substantive corrections needed. Minor point: in §48 the image reads 'numerus b/g notabiliter fuerit minor, quam 4000', which the transcription has correctly.
